extracted.intended_audience: instructional designers, online course editors (MIDEs), educational developers, and academic managers involved in online course design and delivery
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for the multimedia instructional design editor (MIDE) role in designing, editing, evaluating, and producing online course materials, and for financial decision-making about technology in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner-centred course materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Course materials for distance education should 'take a learner-centred approach, rather than the traditional content-centred approach of text-books' and enable students to become involved, motivated, and to take ownership of skills and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials should motivate, engage, direct, and support learners; they are key to motivating and supporting students in distance contexts and therefore must be designed from the learner's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of an online learning environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The online learning environment should encourage a reduction in the didactic role of the teacher, emphasize collaboration, enable development of process skills and knowledge building rather than only information acquisition, and support collaborative group activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices should prioritize collaboration, process skills, and opportunities for knowledge building accessible anytime and from any place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider technical and logistical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must consider resource and time requirements, technology constraints, longevity, currency, and applicability of learning tools and materials; students expect web-access, services access, and communication capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance desired pedagogical features with available resources, platform capabilities, and institutional service expectations (e.g., registrar, library access). Consider continuous-intake models (self-paced or paced group seminars) when designing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of multimedia
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimedia provides 'artful interaction between learners and content' and is especially well suited to dynamic fields, but effectively designed multimedia often requires many resources, significant production/testing time, and increased staff knowledge and workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select multimedia where pedagogically justified; evaluate production and maintenance costs and staff capacity; prioritize multimedia that demonstrably enhances learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage tool diversity and instructional purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much diversity of tools to offer, what instructional purposes each tool serves, and how selected tools will be managed within the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each tool for its instructional value, fit with course objectives, longevity, and maintainability; avoid adding tools without clear pedagogical purpose or manageable maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance learner/instructor control with standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide learners and instructors with choices and control over their learning environment while adhering to institutional instructional standards and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow flexibility where it supports learning, but ensure that choices do not undermine consistent quality, alignment with objectives, or accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent editorial and instructional design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: MIDEs must apply precise editorial and instructional design standards across various course components even as multiple participants revise content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency despite multiple authors and frequent revisions; use standards to ensure pedagogical quality, consistency of presentation, and institutional alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: MIDE role in multimedia development and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: MIDEs identify appropriate locations for multimedia and interactive components, integrate them into templates, explore new ideas, and identify components with widespread applicability for reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work as a liaison among academics, production teams, and departments to develop storage and reuse strategies (learning objects, databases); prioritize components that can be reused to improve efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of instructional design evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: New or significantly revised courses undergo preliminary instructional assessment at proposal stage, but the bulk of MIDE evaluation occurs after the course has been written or revised and is submitted for editing and production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform cursory ID at proposal to guide authors, but plan for deeper ID review later in production to address instructional quality without restarting development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course-level alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: At the course level, determine if course components support and conform to the overall course objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every module, resource, and activity can be traced back to course objectives and contributes to the intended learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit-level objective alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: At the unit level, ensure unit objectives support, build toward, and align with the larger course objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check progressive scaffolding across units so that learning builds logically toward course goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objectives clarity and measurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each learning objective in each unit or lesson must be clear, unambiguous, measurable, and related to the content in the lesson or unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite vague objectives into measurable statements; ensure assessment and activities directly measure these objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate information resources from learning activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Components intended to present/deliver information must be clearly differentiated from learning activities designed for application or practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly label resources vs activities; state the purpose of each activity and make it obvious what action is required, where to submit work, and how/when feedback will be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and functionality of learning resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The MIDE must determine if learning resources work as intended and if instructions for their use are clear, particularly for multimedia components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test interactive/multimedia elements for functionality, usability, and accessibility; provide step-by-step usage instructions and troubleshooting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing for grammar, tone, and online-readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must ensure course text is grammatically correct, concise, online-ready, and that tone is appropriate for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy-edit content for clarity and concision; adapt prose for online reading (scannability, headings, short paragraphs); ensure consistent voice across coauthored materials as desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure intellectual property and ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors ensure course materials do not contain bias or plagiarism and that all necessary copyright clearances have been obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify citations, permissions for third-party media, and that content adheres to institutional ethical/policy standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate learner information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-edited course materials should anticipate and address learner concerns and information needs, preventing 'back end' support calls and building student confidence and satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear assignment instructions, marking guidelines, exam instructions, and guidance on where/how to get help; reduce ambiguity that leads to support demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: MIDE as communicator and transformer
rubrics_metrics.description: MIDEs facilitate communication between authors, learners, and technical staff; they act as transformers who can liaise with subject specialists, distill key ideas, and re-express them in ways learners will understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage actively with all stakeholders, translate technical/disciplinary content into learner-friendly language, and recommend presentation strategies that aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control and institutional standards enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The MIDE's chief contribution is quality control: ensuring rigorous institutional, instructional, and aesthetic standards are applied while balancing learner/instructor flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use checklists and review processes to maintain consistent presentation, currency, and pedagogical soundness; monitor ongoing changes to preserve standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human oversight of content quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology cannot automate the creation of quality content; human editorial and instructional review is necessary to ensure quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on rapid online-editing workflows; schedule human review cycles for substantive content and multimedia before release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define cost objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost objects are items for which a separate measurement of costs is desired (e.g., courses, registration services, projects, students, departments, academic programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly specify cost object(s) before classifying or allocating costs to ensure meaningful financial analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify direct costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct costs can be associated with a cost object in a cost-effective manner; they are usually material, linked to a specific area or responsibility, or related by contract. Rule of thumb: would the cost disappear if the cost object were eliminated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify salaries, software, or materials that would cease if the course/program were discontinued and treat these as direct costs in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify indirect costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect costs do not bear a discernible relationship to a particular cost object, or cannot be determined cost-effectively (e.g., institution-wide insurance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop an allocation method for indirect costs when attributing them to cost objects (discussed further in cost-allocation sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fixed and variable costs and determine relevant range
rubrics_metrics.description: Variable costs change with activity level (e.g., per-student textbooks); fixed costs remain unchanged over a given period (e.g., instructor salary for the year). All costs may vary over wider ranges, so determine the relevant range when categorizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using unit costs that mix fixed and variable components; analyze expected activity ranges to classify costs appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading per-unit cost comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Per-unit costs that include fixed-cost components can misinform decisions (example: fixed $600 vs $30 per student depending on enrolment levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute costs across anticipated enrollment scenarios; choose fixed or variable purchase options based on projected volumes and break-even points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–volume–profit (CVP) analysis assumptions and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: CVP analysis predicts net revenue by calculating total contribution margin (total revenue less total variable costs) then net revenue (contribution margin less fixed costs). It assumes (1) total costs can be divided into fixed and variable components; (2) behaviour of total revenues and costs is linear in the range under consideration; (3) selling price and variable cost per unit are known; (4) time value of money is ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CVP to calculate break-even points and to evaluate the financial implications of enrolment or pricing changes, recognizing the assumptions and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break-even calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Break-even in units = Total Fixed Costs / Per-unit Contribution Margin (selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formula to determine minimum enrollment to cover fixed costs; use example calculations (Course A and B) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contribution margin for decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing between courses or offerings, compare contribution margin per student (revenue minus variable cost) to identify which option increases net revenue before fixed-cost thresholds are reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct additional students to offerings with higher contribution margins until doing so would trigger additional fixed costs (e.g., hiring another instructor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment margin analysis (direct vs indirect fixed costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment margin analysis separates fixed costs into course-specific (direct) and shared/central (indirect) components to determine whether a course should be offered when enrollment is below break-even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate fixed-cost components to see which costs would disappear if a course were cancelled; make continuation decisions based on contribution after removing avoidable fixed costs.
